To the Editor:
Re “
Listening While White
” (column, July 17), written in the form of a letter to Ta-Nehisi Coates about his new book, “Between the World and Me”:
David Brooks just couldn’t help himself. He just had to tell Mr. Coates where he was wrong.
The African-Americans I know would say this drives them crazy when they talk about being black in America. Over and over, whites ask their opinion about their experience of race, and once they get it proceed to disagree.
Mr. Brooks would have done everyone, including himself, a great service if he had just said, “This man has spoken his truth profoundly and I need to respect it by just listening closely and keeping my mind open and my mouth shut for a while.”
But of course he, and white America, just can’t help themselves, just can’t have a conversation about race that doesn’t disrespect another’s truth. It’s one of those things that African-Americans live with every day but white Americans just don’t get.
“Maybe the right white response is just silence for a change,” he asks at the end of the column. Yes, Mr. Brooks, that is the right response.
MARK TRAUTWEIN
San Anselmo, Calif.
To the Editor:
I came away from this column understanding better how identity-wrenching it is for us privileged-while-white Americans to “sit with it, to make sure the [African-American] testimony is respected and sinks in.” We must suffer as we begin to feel how deeply and unrelentingly the system of American society has hurt generation after generation of African-Americans, from the days of slavery into the present.
It is unsettling to think that for an entire group of Americans, the “American dream” may simply not exist. We need to sit with that discomfort, too. Every day black Americans wake up knowing that before they do anything, they will be judged by large swaths of the society as less worthy, less trustworthy, less deserving, less valuable than their nonblack fellow Americans. If we whites find that reality unsettling, imagine what it must feel like to live it out, day after day after day.
ISABEL A. SHERIDAN
Portland, Ore.

CLEVELAND —  Cleveland has reached a settlement with the Justice Department over what federal authorities said was a pattern of unconstitutional policing and excessive use of force, people briefed on the case said Monday.
The settlement, which could be announced as early as Tuesday, comes days after a judge declared a Cleveland police officer
not guilty of manslaughter
in the fatal shooting of a car’s two unarmed occupants, both of them black.
The verdict prompted a day and night of protests and reignited discussions about how police officers treat the city’s African-American residents.
The details of the settlement were not immediately clear, but in similar talks in recent years, the Justice Department has required cities to allow independent monitors to oversee changes in police departments. Settlements are typically backed by court orders and often call for improved training and revised policies for the use of force.
A spokeswoman for the Cleveland Division of Police referred questions to the mayor’s office, which would not comment on Monday. Dena Iverson, a spokeswoman for the Justice Department, also had no comment.
The Justice Department opened an inquiry into the Cleveland police force months after the 2012 shooting of the unarmed occupants in a car, and issued its report in December. Cleveland is among several cities, including Ferguson, Mo., New York and Baltimore, that have become focal points of a national debate over policing and race.
On Saturday, demonstrators spent hours marching through Cleveland after a judge acquitted Officer Michael Brelo of manslaughter for his role in the 2012 shooting, which began with a police chase of the car. While several officers fired a combined 137 shots, Officer Brelo was singled out for manslaughter charges because he climbed onto the hood of the car after the pursuit ended and fired 15 shots into the vehicle.
The occupants, Timothy Russell and Malissa Williams, died from gunshot wounds. The judge ruled that the actions of Officer Brelo, who is white, were lawful.
Cleveland’s streets have stayed calm
since Saturday, when the police reported 71 arrests, some on felony charges.
Dozens of protesters appeared in court here Monday on misdemeanor charges. Some still wore T-shirts with messages like “I Can’t Breathe,” a reference to Eric Garner, who died after being put in a police chokehold in Staten Island last year, and “Black Lives Matter.”
For Cleveland, a settlement with the Justice Department averts a long and costly court fight and the appearance that city leaders are resisting change. Mayor Frank Jackson
faces a recall petition
from city activists who say, among other grievances, that he has not done enough to prevent police abuses.
The Justice Department has called Mr. Jackson a full partner in its effort to improve the police force.
The Justice Department has opened nearly two dozen investigations into police departments under the Obama administration. Federal investigators found patterns of unconstitutional policing in cities including Seattle, Newark, Albuquerque and Ferguson. Federal authorities recently announced they would investigate the Baltimore police after Freddie Gray, a 25-year-old black man, died of injuries he suffered while in custody.

In Seattle, the federal inquiry led local officials to overhaul training and focus on how officers can calm tense situations without using force. In Albuquerque, city officials agreed to change the way the police are trained, outfit officers with body cameras and improve how the department investigates officer-involved shootings.
Officials in Ferguson are negotiating a possible settlement over accusations that officers routinely violated the Constitution.
The Justice Department’s report on the Cleveland police was among its most scathing, finding that they engaged in a pattern of “unreasonable and unnecessary use of force.”
Investigators said officers unnecessarily used deadly force; used excessive force against mentally ill people; and inappropriately resorted to
stun guns
, chemical sprays and punches.
It detailed tactical blunders, and said officers too often imperiled bystanders when they used force.
The Justice Department also criticized a “structurally flawed” discipline policy that it said made it too hard to punish officers for improperly using force.
The report highlighted one case in which officers kicked an African-American man in the head while he was handcuffed and on the ground, then did not report having used force during the arrest.
“Supervisors throughout the chain of command endorse questionable and sometimes unlawful conduct by officers,” Vanita Gupta, the Justice Department’s top civil rights prosecutor, said in December. “Officers are not provided with adequate training, policy guidance and supervision to do their jobs safely and effectively.”
The report was compiled too early to cover the death of 12-year-old Tamir Rice, who was playing with a replica gun in a Cleveland park in November when the police shot him. Prosecutors have yet to decide whether to charge officers in his death or in the case of Tanisha Anderson, 37, who died after she was restrained in a prone position on the pavement.
Most of the protesters arraigned Monday were charged with refusal to disperse, and 35 pleaded no contest to an amended charge of disorderly conduct, which carries no jail time. Twenty people pleaded not guilty and will contest the charges. More protesters are expected to appear in court on Tuesday.
Talis Gage, 31, a Cleveland native now living in a different part of Ohio, was among those who pleaded no contest and was released Monday morning. As with others who pleaded no contest, he was sentenced to time served and was not issued a fine. Mr. Gage said he joined the Saturday protest because he believed that Officer Brelo was guilty of a crime.
“What happened was not justice,” Mr. Gage said outside the courthouse shortly after his release. “It was unfair for this man to walk away with no jail time at all.”

The religious exception bill pending in Arkansas hasn’t just added to the growing debate over what proponents call “religious freedom bills,” which grant people, and businesses, the right to avoid a fine or lawsuit for refusing to obey a state mandate that violates their religious beliefs. It’s brought our attention squarely back to one of the big divides in politics: When it comes to things like gay rights (and education spending, immigration, and the environment),
the generation gap is back
.
When that gap becomes a family rift, politics become personal. When Gov. Asa Hutchinson, Republican of Arkansas, spoke  earlier this week about the future of the religious exemption bill in his state, he disclosed that
the proposal had drawn resistance from a place close to home: his son, Seth Hutchinson
.
Both father and son insist that their differences, which the younger Mr. Hutchinson says evolved over time, haven’t affected their relationship. Instead, “robust discussions” and “lively and engaging conversations” still leave them close (if that’s true, I know many families that would envy them). Now, it’s Gov. Hutchinson whose views appear to be evolving; he has called on lawmakers in his state
to either recall or amend the legislation
. His son takes no credit for the change, but credit can probably be given to the larger cross-generational, cross-partisan conversation that’s grown too loud to ignore in past weeks.
What’s happening there? For the best explanation of the religious exemption bills themselves, their history, and the political debate surrounding them, check out this
Q and A from Erik Ekholm
. But the dinner table conversation for families gathering this holiday weekend is simpler, and if you’re likely to find yourself in mid-debate over a Passover or Easter meal, it’s worth it to try to understand where the other side is coming from.
These bills aren’t nominally about gay marriage, but the debate around them for individuals tends to be. Oddly, there’s pretty clear common ground: Both those who object to the bills and those who support them want what can loosely be termed freedom, but they see the threat to that freedom in very different ways. If you, as a potential member of a weekend family debate team, can look to that freedom question, it may be possible to turn the temperature down around the table, even among people with heated views about the larger issue.
Supporters of religious exemption bills don’t see why a florist, baker or pizza shop should have to help in the celebration of something that offends their religious beliefs, particularly given that there are likely to be other providers of those services who are more than willing to step in. To take the broadest view of that position, they may not see themselves as opposing gay marriage or civil rights. They just think that subset of religious believers should be allowed to do their thing without limits on how they do it.
Those offended by the bills don’t see why a florist, baker or pizza shop that’s open to the public should be allowed to choose whom they serve, particularly given the echoes of racial discrimination that those “choices” evoke. To take the broadest view of that position, they may not see themselves as advocating for interference against religious beliefs. They just think that all people hosting legal weddings should be allowed to do their thing without limits on how they do it.
Of course, those descriptions of two opposing points of view are dramatically over-simplified; passionate advocates on either side of this issue likely have both more complex and narrower views. But stepping back to take the most generous look at those you’re debating might help to turn conversations from crushing and infuriating to “lively and engaging.” If you’re on either side at the holiday table this coming weekend, how do you think it will go, and are these debates going to continue will into 2016?

JABUGO, Spain —  On a vast farm dotted with oak and cork trees, about 350 pigs are enjoying the final weeks of a short but blissful life. They roam freely, sleep outdoors or shelter in spacious pigsties. Above all, autumn is when they get to feast all day on acorns recently fallen from the trees.
“Pigs are known for eating everything, but when it comes to their favorite acorns, they are real connoisseurs and very selective — and the sweeter the acorn, the better,” said Juan Carlos Domínguez Lorenzo, 49, who was born on the farm and has been looking after its pigs since he was a teenager.
The way these pigs of
Spain
’s Ibérico breed are fed and raised here is a far cry from how most meats are produced almost anywhere, making the cured ham a delicacy prized for its unique texture and taste, which is enhanced by the sweet and nutty flavor of the acorns the pigs eat.
So when the World Health Organization, in a recent report, linked
processed meats to colorectal cancer
, the news came as an affront to many Spaniards, who have been eating cured hams produced this way for generations.
Today,
Spain
’s Ibérico hams are increasingly sought after worldwide, particularly among Chinese consumers concerned about the safety of their own homegrown food.
“Spanish ham is a very unique product, but it’s also seen as healthy, which is a real asset when you’re selling to the Chinese,” said Oliver Win of Olivier Pacific Limited, a fine foods distribution company based in Hong Kong that imports the Cinco Jotas brand of Spanish ham.
Spain’s producers, in fact, took no small measure of umbrage at the World Health Organization’s attempt to lump their luxury ham together with cheaper products like processed sausages and hamburger meat.
A single leg of the finest ham from Cinco Jotas — weighing almost 18 pounds — costs about $670 in Spain. (In the United States, the price is about double.) Even the way
the ham is sliced
is considered something of an art form.
“This ham is as natural as food can get — no added heavy metals, preservatives or colorings — and it comes from an animal that has built up muscle by eating the best food and exercising a lot in beautiful surroundings,” said José Gómez, the owner of Joselito, another top brand of ham. “There are thousands of products that present a higher cancer risk.”

China

In fact, the Chinese appetite for Spanish pork stretches all the way down its production chain, including innards that Spanish companies struggle to export to many Western countries.
Fresh pork exports to

Last year, Fosun, one of China’s largest financial and industrial conglomerates, bought a stake in the parent company of Cinco Jotas, one of Spain’s top brands of Ibérico ham, which is based in Jabugo.
“We generally think that our culture is closer to that of America, but when it comes to ham, Chinese gastronomy is really in tune with ours,” Bernardino Rodríguez, the general director of Cinco Jotas, said during a tour of cellars where legs of ham are hooked from the ceiling and left to age.
“I can’t think of anybody more capable of distinguishing between different qualities of ham than the Chinese,” he said.
But the health and quality of the animals have also become a big driver of Chinese demand. Early this year, the Chinese police arrested more than 110 people who were accused of trafficking pork from diseased pigs.
“Many Chinese come and buy food in Hong Kong and have turned it into a parallel import market largely because of their safety worries about food in China,” Mr. Win, the importer, said.
Paradoxically, however, the same things that have lured the Chinese about the natural way the pigs here are raised, slaughtered and cured are some of the chief sources of tension between Spain’s producers and the United States.
Ibérico ham was banned in the United States until about a decade ago over concerns about swine fever and traditional curing methods, and even today just a handful of Spanish slaughterhouses have been authorized to export to the United States.
Today, Francisco Espárrago, the chairman of Señorío de Montanera, a midsize producer of ham, said he found it much easier to get Chinese importers, as opposed to those in the United States, to view Spain’s best ham as a luxury product.
“The Americans believe that everything should follow their own processes, so they don’t seem to understand that allowing the ham to sweat in the heat spreads the flavor but doesn’t destroy the meat,” he said. “For the Chinese, that concept isn’t a problem.”
The finest Ibérico ham is produced in southwestern Spain, a region that also has strong weather changes.
For instance, Jabugo has some of Spain’s heaviest rainfalls, resulting in a damp winter climate that helps spread the salt into the meat as it is cured, using a method dating to Roman times. The hot summer months, in contrast, favor the so-called sweating and drying of the ham.
“If you don’t have the right climate, you simply can’t produce,” Mr. Gómez of Joselito said. “Ham is a bit like wine, because several small steps and adjustments make all the difference between an average product and premium quality.”
The growing Chinese fascination with the hams has also been helped by an increase in Chinese visitors to Spain, where they have the opportunity to taste firsthand the country’s wide array of pork-related gastronomy.
“We open at 1 p.m., and the first clients who then cross the door are now almost certainly Chinese,” said José María Ruiz Benito, the owner of the eponymous José María restaurant in Segovia, famous for its roasted suckling pig.
As a result, some producers are also wary about sharing their skills with China, noting that a few years ago Spain already had to pressure the Chinese authorities to stop some producers from breaching copyright rules by labeling their ham as “Jabugo.”
“My worry is that the Chinese are willing to import today so that they can work out how to produce their own great ham tomorrow,” said Ricardo Sánchez, managing director of Arturo Sánchez, a Spanish producer.
For now, however, the idea that his pigs will end up on Chinese plates seems very remote to Mr. Domínguez Lorenzo, the farmer.
“I make everything right for these pigs, and if that work is recognized on the other side of the world, that’s just fine,” he said.
He then turned toward his pigs and produced a loud “tuueeeeh!” to draw their attention, before leading them, almost like a shepherd, toward another clump of trees in search of freshly fallen acorns.

The polymath
Pierre Klossowski
was a venerable figure of the last century: novelist, translator and hero of the philosophers
Michel Foucault and Gilles Deleuze
. In the art world, however, he remains a lesser-known quantity, especially on this side of the Atlantic. Though his airy Mannerist-influenced drawings have appeared in museum retrospectives in London, Paris and Cologne, Germany, as well as in major group exhibitions like Documenta, Klossowski has been overshadowed in the United States by his younger brother, the painter
Balthus
(né Balthasar Klossowski).
But the elder is the more compelling artist. Balthus’s scenes of jaded nymphets display an indifference to history and ideas that verges on revanchism. In Pierre’s art, especially the large figurative drawings he began making in middle age, eroticism is just one of many interlocking concerns: modernity, hospitality, violence, self-conception. Nine of these awkward but engrossing drawings — dating from 1979 to 1990, many featuring his aggressed but steadfast female character Roberte in compromising positions — are on view now in the new uptown branch of Gladstone Gallery. By any account they are unmissable, though you will want to leave the kids at home for this one.
Klossowski was born in 1905 in Paris; his Polish father was an art historian, and his mother was a student of Bonnard. Pierre and Balthasar, three years younger, moved to Berlin just as World War I began; their parents split up, thanks in part to their mother’s
affair
with Rainer Maria Rilke.
It was Rilke who introduced Pierre to André Gide, for whom he served as a secretary. The young Klossowski helped edit “The Counterfeiters” as well as “Corydon,” Gide’s bold 1924 defense of homosexuality, which drew heavily on contemporary sexology. A drawing here offers a hint of what Klossowski might have learned from his mentor: A young Greek athlete, naked but for his golden sandals, gazes up from a locker room bench to receive the benediction of Socrates while half a dozen other men look on.
Bilingual, Klossowski translated several major works of German philosophy into French, among them Nietzsche’s “The Gay Science” and Walter Benjamin’s “The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction.” Sade, especially, was an influence. In the shadow of the Holocaust, Klossowski published “Sade Mon Prochain” (“Sade My Neighbor,” 1947), a study of desire and unreason, and then “Roberte ce Soir” a Sadean fusion of novel and philosophy in which the titular heroine is ordered by her husband to sleep with a series of guests.
But in “Roberte ce Soir” and in the subsequent drawings on view here, sex is not especially dramatic, nor does submission look especially dolorous. Roberte — who in the novel is no feeble girl, like those brother Balthus liked to paint, but a radical member of Parliament — appears serene in a long, narrow drawing featuring her trussed between parallel bars, wearing a pageboy cap but no underwear. In another drawing she is splayed out nude on the lap of a medieval hero, but her stern mien expresses contentment and self-command.

Sex is neither a joy nor a punishment in these drawings, but a ritualized encounter governed by complex rules of hospitality. Klossowski’s soft palette — mauve and orchid and powder blue and beige — compounds the sense of quiet, as does his languorous figuration: Roberte is extruded like one of Parmigianino’s long-necked sitters, while a boy on roller skates has legs as spindly and disproportionate as a flamingo’s. Where Balthus strove for academic precision in his drawings, Pierre drew more freely and more surreally. You may be reminded more of the sexed-up Surrealism of Max Ernst and Hans Bellmer, though Klossowski’s drawings are more uneasy.
The model for many of the drawings of Roberte was Klossowski’s
wife, Denise
— a member of the French Resistance who was deported to the Ravensbruck concentration camp in Germany, then escaped. And indeed the legacy of World War II, and the proof it gave of modernity’s easy descent into atrocity, linger in the background of Klossowski’s writing and art. In the 1980 drawing “La Belle Empoisonneuse,” we see a woman in a bourgeois bedroom pushing a goblet toward her shocked husband’s mouth. Grabbing her from behind is a strange hooded figure in red: the devil, perhaps, or an executioner. Even stranger is a disembodied hand that extends from the right of the picture plane — an informant’s. For Klossowski, as for Sade before him, the everyday couple or everyday family was the true abomination, and the likelier source of violence. It was only in extremity that civilization could be preserved.
It took many years, and a model of art history that stopped seeing the past as a mere succession of avant-gardes, before Klossowski finally won attention in Europe as a visual artist. I hope the same happens here. To mount an exhibition of such an unsung European artist counts as a statement of intent from Gladstone Gallery, which is inaugurating its Upper East Side space with this important show. And there is far more to explore: Klossowski was also a filmmaker, and played the lead in a screen adaptation of “Roberte ce Soir.”
One last thing: Architectural aficionados should make a special trek. The new gallery is housed in a
townhouse designed by Edward Durell Stone
, a landmark of International Style now happily open to the public. Stone, one of the two architects of the original Museum of Modern Art, replaced the front of the townhouse in 1956 with an imposing, even pitiless facade of round concrete baffles. On the parlor level, the interior features a marble floor and ample natural light — an Apollonian setting for some of the last century’s greatest Dionysian drawings.

A show unlikely to please the shy, the claustrophobic or those with weak calf muscles,
“Mrs. Mayfield’s Fifth-Grade Class of ’93 20-Year Reunion”
takes place in an apartment on the fifth floor of an East Village walk-up. Whose apartment? Unclear, though certificates on the walls congratulate her on her mastery of ear candling and reiki.
Sweet and boisterous, this site-specific, immersive performance by Caps Lock Theater casts the members of its audience as fellow reunion guests. “Whether you’re 18 or 80, you are 30 years old and you were in Mrs. Mayfield’s fifth-grade class of 1993,” a sheet of printed rules explains. The host, Amanda (Diana Oh), recently single and unemployed, has decided to get the old pre-tween gang together for an evening of booze, reminiscence and
“Whoomp! (There It Is).”
On arriving, you can choose a green name tag, if you want characters to talk to you (the interaction is pretty gentle), or a red one if you don’t. Beer and wine are available for $5 to help you get into the party mood, and so is free chili, though I saw only one audience member partaking. She seemed to enjoy it.
The director, Leta Tremblay, stages scenes in every room of the apartment and on the roof, too — often simultaneously, so you have to decide which to follow. Whatever you miss is likely to be clarified later. And the space is small enough that you can probably position yourself to listen to two scenes at once.
You’ll hear and see flirtation and revelation, breakups and make-ups and a fair amount of making out. While several audience members were in the bedroom, the bow-tied, chili-bearing Jamie (Jesse Geguzis) rushed in from the living room and said, “If this is a sex party, there really ought to be condoms provided.” Everyone ran out to see. (A note to the prudish: This part isn’t participatory, and everyone remains basically clothed.)
The plot is clichéd, and so are many of the characters. “Mrs. Mayfield’s” has clearly been created through improvisation, then assembled into a script by the playwright Mariah MacCarthy. Yet a lot of the dialogue still sounds stagy rather than spontaneous, which you can’t help noticing when the character speaking it is sitting thigh-to-thigh with you on a sofa. The acting, and ad-libbing, are variable.
But you’d be surprised how little of this matters. The show can’t boast the square footage or the design budget or the top-shelf liquor of an extravaganza like “Sleep No More,” but “Mrs. Mayfield’s” still feels like an adventure and an event.
“This party was a lovely thought,” one character says, “if vastly misguided and incredibly inappropriate.” And a lot of fun, too.

The Oscar nominations are upon us, the ceremony is 38 days away, and a few surprises may yet lie in store in the newly narrowed universe of possible outcomes.
One thing is certain: Within days if not hours of the last statue passing hands, prognosticators will be drawing up lists — they probably already have — forecasting likely nominees for next year. Less than 72 hours after last year’s ceremony,
lists emerged
for this year that were both on the mark and wildly off. They included what turned out to be the shoo-ins, “Boyhood” and “The Imitation Game,” longer shots (“Unbroken,” “Gone Girl” and “Interstellar” — we’ll know their fate Thursday) as well as non-starters (“Jersey Boys”).
How do these people know, do they really know and why the need to predict a year out, at a time when post-awards-season recovery will have barely begun? And who are these prognosticators anyway?
Reader, they are Oscarologists, and they populate a small reportorial subuniverse that fully came into existence only a decade ago. Denizens of this world include, but are not limited to, a mélange of former show business and music journalists, film enthusiasts and kooky pontificators, working at or running sites and outlets that include Awards Daily, Deadline Hollywood, Fandango, Gold Derby, Grantland, HitFix, Hollywood Elsewhere, The Hollywood Reporter, Indiewire, The Los Angeles Times, Movie City News, Variety, The Wrap, and, yes, The New York Times.
Some are more respected than others. Some are considered crazy. Some are viewed as the studios’ handmaidens. But whether they — we — like it not, all are more or less chasing the same news in the same new world, and the studios are paying attention.
“I remember a decade ago calling a studio publicist for an interview, and when I said I was an Oscar blogger, she essentially laughed in my face,” said Scott Feinberg, who covers awards for the trade paper The Hollywood Reporter. “Meanwhile, 10 years later, for better or worse, we are quite valued.”
Continue reading the main story
“Valued” is one way to describe the tricky and invariably incestuous relationship between Oscar bloggers and the studios and awards news they ostensibly cover.
Many awards sites are largely dependent on the “For Your Consideration” ads that court Academy voters, and also on access to film stars, directors and the like. In this highly transactional world, ticking off the wrong person with less-than-laudatory reporting could mean getting cut off outright.
“I don’t confer with the Oscar campaigners that much,” said Anne Thompson, a longtime show business journalist who now covers the awards season for
Indiewire.com
, which focuses on independent film. “My job isn’t to carry water for them. My job is to really share with my readers what I think they need to know.”
Later, she added: “But IndieWire totally gets Oscar advertising, no question about it. I’m walking a very fine line.”
David Poland of
Movie City News
has a more cynical view. “I respect and disrespect almost everyone in this game,” he said. Garnering nominations has become part of movie campaigns, which involves getting pieces written about a given production. “There’s almost no news in the business — it’s almost all publicity — but that’s become the dominant driver,” he said. “This is the way of keeping everyone in line, by keeping everyone alive.”
Continue reading the main story
By most accounts, the Oscar blogosphere evolved its way into existence in the late 1990s. Perhaps to be expected, there are differing accounts as to who exactly was first. Among them was Sasha Stone, who described herself to the Bagger as “a self appointed expert/total nobody with a 1,200-baud modem,” and started the site Oscar Watch, which later became
Awards Daily
. Tom O’Neil, who said he began tracking awards in the late ’80s, started the site
Gold Derby
, which issued Oscar odds and, Mr. O’Neil said, “drove the studio execs crazy.”
“Both of us watched the industry bloom around us,” Ms. Stone said.
The sites Movie City News and then
Hollywood Elsewhere
, by Jeffrey Wells, soon followed (both men said they began online awards tracking in the late ’90s, too), but the real turning point, Mr. O’Neil said, came around 2005. As print journalism’s ad revenues continued to plummet, The Los Angeles Times licensed and expanded Gold Derby.
“That’s when it got serious,” Mr. O’Neil said. “There were suddenly Oscar pundits everywhere. It was the first time consumer media were competing alongside trade publications for the F.Y.C. ads. That’s what this is all about.”
The sites need a steady stream of content, which is a big reason handicapping takes place so early in the year. The Oscarologists know which films have major studio campaigns behind them, and they know the biases of the Academy. Mr. O’Neil said he is always hassled, most harshly by studio executives, over crystal-balling movies before anyone has seen them. His pat response is that it’s not that dissimilar from forecasting football games: The Oscarologists know the players, their track records and — perhaps more questionably — the odds.
“It’s partly educated guesses and partly the diminishing number of films headed for the Oscar race; that’s the direction Hollywood is moving in,” Ms. Stone said. “Movies are made for this race. And fewer and fewer studios are making movies like this.”
She added later: “The fix is in; it’s not rocket science. They’re already designed to be just that.”
Mr. Wells of Hollywood Elsewhere said a primal form of wishful thinking also drives forecasters’ lists.
“There’s a preordained desire to see certain people at least be nominated,” he said. “You have to have a really honest look at the basic impulse to show obeisance before power and glamour. People want Brangelina to be a part of the conversation.”
Of course a major downside of early prognostication is the deleterious effect that high expectations can have on movies, including, this year, Angelina Jolie’s “Unbroken.” That film and “Interstellar” topped many forecasters’ lists months before anyone had gotten a peek at either film and then tumbled in the rankings after screenings (despite being box-office winners).
“Everything is built up, built up, built up, and then we can tear it down, tear it down, tear it down,” said Pete Hammond, who writes for
Deadline Hollywood
. “I don’t think it helps movies much.”

There are several Oscarologists who have sunnier views of this line of work. Mr. Feinberg, a longtime movie fan, began making annual Oscar lists in high school and said he remained delighted at getting paid for doing something he loves and used to do for free. “Everyone gets too jaded,” he said. “There are a lot of worse beats.”
And Kyle Buchanan, who covers the awards season for New York magazine’s entertainment site,
Vulture
, holds the view, shared by many, that the Oscars help ensure that quality films get made in a cinematic landscape saturated with comic book movies.
“I don’t think that Oscar coverage obviates actual critical discussion,” Mr. Buchanan said. “The idea that ‘Boy, something is really wrong when people care this much about what happens at the Oscars’ is a straw-man argument.”
Yet perhaps inevitably, within the cloistered world of Oscarology, where everyone is rabidly hungry for new tidbits and anxious to be first, information is bounced around, repeated and amplified.
“You get a kind of echo-chamber buzz that consists of people talking about what their colleagues are talking about,” said Steve Pond, a former Rolling Stone journalist who now writes about film awards for The Wrap. “I’m not sure that contributes much to what I think my job is, which is to cover this circus as a journalist.”
And, every year, the circus ends the same way. “It’s crazy,” Mr. Pond said. “You spend all this time writing about what essentially is going to be three and a half hours of television and 24 people getting statues. And you think: ‘Wow. That’s six months of my life.’ ”

“Mom, when do grown-ups stop eating breakfast?”
It was late in the afternoon. It had been hours since breakfast. Hours even since lunch. The sun was already setting on another busy day of school, karate car pools, soccer and ballet. There were reading logs to complete, math facts to review, and “What’s for dinner?” could be heard in rumbly tummies all over the house.
She was poking around in the pantry, looking for something healthy to fill her growing body. She’s 8, and her question from within the shelves of cereal boxes and bags of chips reminded me that not much escapes her attention. Mistakenly, I thought I had.
My hands, coated in a mixture of raw ground beef, breadcrumbs and egg, stilled in the bowl. The meat was barely defrosted and I could feel the ribbons of a brain-freeze tighten behind my eyes.
I couldn’t ignore her question. Even though I wanted to.
The easy answer, the obvious answer, is: never. Grown-ups never stop eating breakfast, no matter their age. All people, babies, toddlers, children and adults, need to eat good, nutritional food for breakfast, lunch and dinner with a few healthy and not-so-healthy snacks in between. Food is where we get energy to keep our brains and bodies working. And that’s the answer.
But I don’t eat breakfast. I haven’t for years. Decades. And I’m the grown-up she watches closely, every morning, not eating breakfast. I bustle around the kitchen, making it for her and her brothers. Waffles, toast and jelly, glasses of milk and orange juice.
I pack their school lunches, slather cream cheese on slice after slice of bread for sandwiches, count out string cheese, yogurt, bags of cookies, pretzels, juice boxes, grapes. There is food everywhere, cereal spilled out on the counter top and cookie crumbs all over the floor. I sip my tea.
I was 17 when I stopped eating breakfast. And lunch. And dinner. And anything in between. A college sophomore, I missed my boyfriend, my parents, and the safe cocoon of life at home where I understood who I was and why. The refusal to eat quickly became the way I could control the confused and confusing feelings that raged inside me.
My journalism class was competitive. The drama department was ruthless. I had come from a small high school where academic excellence, starring roles and a trophy for the best monologue were easy to come by. But now I was one of dozens who loved to write and be in the spotlight. My greatest role at college was the hippopotamus in a children’s production of Rudyard Kipling’s “How the Elephant Got Its Trunk.” The director insisted I wear huge, clumsy rain boots on my feet and hands to enlarge my frail, un-hippo-like presence on stage.
Bewildered by this feeling that I was alone and unknown on a campus teeming with self-awareness, ambition and motivation, I counted calories and increased my exercise. The steady beat of my running shoes pounding the quiet roads at the break of every day was more tolerable to hear than the ever-present, unrealized cries for recognition echoing in my heart.
Surrounded by friends and parties, I felt dark and invisible.
At first I didn’t know. I didn’t know not eating would mean weakness, and darkness. I didn’t know my spine would get so bony it would hurt to do those energetic rolls on the stage floor in drama class. I didn’t know my hip bones would stick out. Or that three bones would lie like clear, shining stripes above my breastbone. I liked seeing the bones of my body. Sharp and clear. Arms and wrists like fragile, brittle twigs. I didn’t know my hair would get straggly. Dead ends. I didn’t know my period, my life force, would stop. Dry up.
I didn’t know I would be cold all the time.
And I didn’t know I would like it. I liked the darkness, the emptiness. I liked feeling empty, a big, blank canvas upon which anything could happen. It felt like all my colorful imaginings would be possible on that canvas. If only I knew what to imagine. If only I could see myself. One day I weighed 108 pounds. Two days later I weighed 99.
My weight hovered around 100 pounds until I graduated. The desire to feel invisible and noticed at the same time was my closest friend, holding my hand as we walked to class together, sitting next to me in the dining hall, whispering in my ear at parties. I wanted to shrink myself so nobody could see me, to become invisible because I didn’t feel worthy of attention. And I craved attention and hoped somebody would notice me shrinking. It felt like nobody could be bothered to really know me, the real me, deep inside. Even as my best friend fretted over my refusal to eat, even as a loud, giggly girl waiting with me on line for the pay phone jammed her fist into my poky hip and told me I was “disappearing.”
It was me who didn’t know me.
Two decades, 17 years of marriage, four children later, I know who I am and I’m happy with her, most of the time: a writer, a wife, a mom, a daughter, a sister, a friend. I don’t starve myself the way I used to, but when life feels confusing or difficult, as it often does, the first question my husband asks is, “Did you eat today?” My body is no longer anorexic, but sometimes my brain hangs on to that bewildering behavior when I’m out of touch with myself: maybe I drink too much, exercise obsessively, put off meals until the next tomorrow.
And my healthy 8-year-old girl tells me she doesn’t want to be a grown-up because she can never imagine not eating breakfast.
She knows me. And I know me. I know it remains unresolved, but not unnoticed. I still lie in bed every night and run my hands down my hips, feeling for those two sharp bones on either side of my body. I wake up in the morning, feed my family, and then, sometimes, I eat breakfast.

All those pigs-in-a-blanket can get pricey.
Saddled with hundreds of thousands of dollars in catering bills, Hillary Rodham Clinton’s campaign wants to have donors foot the bill for those appetizers and gin-and-tonics -– not to mention valet parking – at some fund-raisers.
She made the unusual request
in a letter
this month to the Federal Election Commission  asking for its legal blessing to offload the expenses without running afoul of campaign finance limits. The request was first
reported by Politico
.
The worry is that if the donors pick up the tab themselves, the F.E.C. might consider that an “in-kind contribution” to Mrs. Clinton’s campaign that would count against the $2,700 they can each contribute to her campaign in the nominating contest. And that, of course, would leave less cash for the donors to contribute to the campaign.
In the request, the campaign wrestled with the distinctly Washington dilemma of how to provide alcohol and nourishment to a roomful of hungry donors.
Marc Elias, a lawyer for the Clinton campaign, argued in the letter to the F.E.C. that if Mrs. Clinton holds a fund-raiser at a hotel or a restaurant – but doesn’t explicitly promise the guests any food or drinks – the donors should be free to buy it themselves without a legal problem.
“Any contrary conclusion here is proven unsound when taken to its logical extreme: if an event  attendee purchases a hot dog at a cart that happens to be set up outside of a campaign event, clearly the payment for the hot dog is not considered an in-kind contribution to the campaign,” Mr. Elias wrote.
“The facts presented here are no different. In each case, the campaign has not provided event  attendees with food or beverages, and the attendee has independently made the decision to eat or drink. Further, in each case, that decision has no impact — financial or otherwise — on the campaign.”
The F.E.C. had no immediate comment.

Grand Army, which opened on Tuesday evening in Boerum Hill in Brooklyn, represents the coming-of-age of the neighborhood’s restaurants — a cocktail bar with only small plates, and nothing repurposed in sight. It’s also the coming-of-age of some restaurateurs: Noah Bernamoff of
Mile End
and Julian Brizzi of
Rucola
, who teamed up with a longtime
Prime Meats
bar director, Damon Boelte, to open in what was once the chrome-plated
Victory Cafe
. (The fourth partner,
Daniel Krieger
, is a photographer who contributes to The New York Times and other publications.)
On Tuesday, as people slipped through the Chilean-print curtain at 336 State Street, three of the partners were on hand. Mr. Brizzi led arrivals through the softly lit space. Mr. Boelte, Willie Nelson-like in his red bandanna and braids, poured railroad-inspired cocktails behind the oyster bar. Mr. Bernamoff expedited orders in the kitchen. “Neighborhood bar” was how he described his aspirations for Grand Army. But not any neighborhood. “Boerum Hill is the best neighborhood in Brooklyn right now,” he said, with the confidence of someone who knew the
Ace Hotel
might be moving in a few blocks away and it didn’t matter; either way, “hip and sophisticated” brownstone dwellers would pay $16 for a poached egg to soften the edge of a Super Chief cocktail.
IN THE SEATS
Seafood dominates the menu, and the exterior and furniture — 30 bar stools, 11 tables and a banquette — are a naval blue. On opening night, families with toddlers and couples took the tables, including David Kaplan and Cat Weaver, but their eyes were on the bar.
Ms. Weaver, 54, who writes
a column about the art market
for Hyperallergic, a cultural website, said: “It’s so Brooklyn here. Everyone is 40 and under. Very casual dress. They’re here to drink.” Mr. Kaplan, 46, who writes for
GeoMarketing, an advertising news site
, responded, “You make it sound like a dive bar.” She clarified: “No, no. It’s understated hip. Not a Williamsburg crowd. No beards.”
WHY THEY CAME
“We live in Sunset Park and we had to check it out,” Mr. Kaplan said. “The reputation of Mile End helped out. Then we were told we could get a table within half an hour, not ‘come back in six months.’ They seated us in 10 minutes.” Ms. Weaver added, “David is my cultural guide and husband, so it was easy for me.”
ON THE PLATES
Mr. Kaplan and Ms. Weaver shared six Peter’s Point and six Bras D’Or oysters ($3.50 each); the bread called miche with shio kombu butter ($8); surryano ham (serrano ham but made in Surry, Va.) with bread-and-butter pickles ($12); asparagus in smoked egg yolk with aged pecorino and bonito flakes ($13); smoked octopus with celeriac, black olives and celery oil ($17); and hamachi with fermented daikon and cilantro ($17). It was “amazing,” Mr. Kaplan said, but at the end of the meal, he returned to the menu. “We ordered a lot, but we didn’t eat a lot,” he said. Ms. Weaver said, “I think women are going to like it, but men are going to want dinner afterward.”
WHAT THEY TALKED ABOUT
Her drive over from Sunset Park, in an Uber vehicle. “My driver had a very heated seat in the car,” she said. “He was a really sweet guy, but I don’t know why he was heating the seat on the nicest day of the year. I’m going to give him five stars, even if he baked my buns.”
And the drinks. From the large selection of beer and cider, he chose the Folksbier Grand Army Stout ($6) and she selected the Greenpoint Acidifus Complex Sour Ale ($6).
“We were just trying to see if there was a ‘Game of Thrones’ reference in the beer name — the Acidifus Complex,” Mr. Kaplan said. “I think it’s more Freudian,” his wife said. What would the Acidifus Complex be? “I think you’d feel guilty about squeezing too many lemons,” Ms. Weaver said.

Social media, that putative engine of destruction in teenage lives, seems to have very little impact on their romances.
A newly released report from the Pew Foundation on
“Teens, Technology and Romantic Relationships”
suggests that for the current group of 13- to 17-year-olds, online communication and social media play a similar role in their lives as the mall did for earlier generations. The digital realm is one place among others to hang out, to display one’s affections, to flirt and express interest and even (although it’s frowned upon) to eventually break up.
The numbers are mildly interesting: Relatively few teenagers (24 percent of teenagers who have had relationship experience or roughly 8 percent of all teenagers) have dated or hooked up with someone they first met online. Of those who have met a partner online, the majority met on social media sites, and the bulk of them met on Facebook. Most (59 percent) of teenage social media users with relationship experience say social media makes them feel more connected to what is happening in their significant other’s life, but 27 percent say social media can make them feel at least somewhat jealous or unsure about their relationship, with 7 percent feeling this way “a lot.” Teenagers frown on breaking up by text or by phone (most say an in-person discussion is the best way), but they do it anyway (27 percent of teenagers with relationship experience have broken up with someone via text message, 31 percent have been broken up with in this way, and the numbers are similar for phone calls).
What is truly striking about the research, however, is the same thing that was most striking about the foundation’s earlier report on
“Teens, Technology and Friendships”
: nothing. For the teenagers responding to this survey and in the later focus groups, technology was just another tool in the box, and the digital world just another space. Though it often helps them feel more connected, it’s no substitute for being together in person, and, that’s it. The drama concerned adults may fear — the romantic partner met online who is dangerous in person, the shame of the public breakup, the stalking ex — is surely present in some teenagers’ lives, but isn’t reflected in the numbers. Over all, the suggestion is one of fully integrated online and offline worlds.
That social integration doesn’t mean teenagers, like adults, aren’t finding themselves caught up in questions of how much of our lives we want to spend in online interactions, and how much those interactions affect the quality of our real experiences. The young people Sherry Turkle described in her article
“Stop Googling, Let’s Talk,”
wanted their parents to put down their phones, and questioned the depth of a conversation conducted phone-in-hand, dipping in and out of both on- and offline worlds.
Teenagers, like adults, want and value their online connection. No one wants to be left out of their friends’ texting conversations. No one wants their friends, or parents or children, to text with others instead of talking to them, either.
What the Pew Foundation’s overall “the kids are all right online” findings suggest isn’t an end to questions about the ways the digital realm colors and shifts real world relationships. Instead, it argues that that conversation shouldn’t be focused on teenagers, but rather on everyone who has ever found herself tempted into Facebook or email at a social gathering. Social media, and all of the rest of what it means to be constantly wired in, may not be the destructive force we once feared, but it is changing us. We should talk (online and off) about how.

There were few outward signs of the thriving heroin stash house that federal officials say was being operated on a quiet block in the Bronx across from Van Cortlandt Park. No one seemed to be permanently living in the apartment, 5E, at 210 West 251st Street, just outside the exclusive Fieldston neighborhood, officials said.
But as federal agents raided the hide-out over the weekend, they upended what they described on Tuesday as a major heroin-importing organization that had ties to an area in Mexico controlled by the Sinaloa Cartel and that had been receiving multimillion-dollar shipments of the drug at least once a month since 2013.
Traffickers from Mexico even visited New York to see things for themselves, taking in the sights and visiting Times Square, officials said.
The seizure on Sunday capped an elaborate yearlong investigation, yielding 70 kilograms of heroin — or nearly 155 pounds — that investigators say came from Mexico and was sold in chunks to various dealers for distribution upstate and across the Northeast.
The seizure, had the drugs been broken down in heroin mills and packaged into $10 envelopes, was enough “to supply a dose of heroin for each and every New York City resident, man, woman and child,” the city’s special narcotics prosecutor, Bridget G. Brennan, said. She estimated the drugs’ street value at roughly $50 million.
According to the federal
Drug Enforcement Administration
, it was the largest seizure of heroin by its agents in the city, and the agency’s fourth largest haul nationwide. Officials said it represented a disruption that would send a message to traffickers, cause dealers to scramble for a supply and, potentially, save lives.
But
it was not the largest amount ever intercepted in the city
. In the late 1960s and early 1970s, two shipments of more than 200 pounds each were seized from cars aboard passenger ships entering the city.
In 1989, federal agents uncovered 849 pounds of heroin in Flushing, Queens
, and in 1991, 1,071 pounds was found in Oakland, Calif.
An automobile was also the method of concealment in the weekend case, which comes amid a resurgence of heroin sales in New York City and elsewhere.
Investigators listening in on a wiretap learned that the drug-importing organization was expecting delivery of another large load over the weekend and set up surveillance outside the apartment on West 251st Street, officials said.
Court documents gave this account:
On Saturday, investigators followed as Yenci Cruz Francisco, 19, steered a late-model Chevrolet Suburban sport utility vehicle from its parking spot in a gated lot behind the Bronx building to an industrial parking lot off Interstate 287 in Montville, N.J.
Trailing the Suburban in a Honda Accord were Jose A. Mercedes, 46, and an unidentified woman. After the vehicles stayed for about an hour in a lot used by tractor-trailers, they headed back to the Bronx — this time with the woman driving the Suburban alone, and the two men following.
After the Suburban returned to the Bronx and was parked behind the apartment building, a drug-sniffing dog detected narcotics in it.

Inside the Suburban, 70 rectangular kilogram packages of heroin, marked with the identifying name “Rolex,” were discovered in a cache built under the floor, officials said.
Investigators also confiscated $2 million in cash under the floorboards of the apartment and a handgun from another location, Ms. Brennan said.
Agents arrested Mr. Mercedes, who is charged with running the operation, and Mr. Francisco, who was charged with drug-trafficking offenses.
In November, they arrested Mr. Mercedes’s son, Jose Mercedes Jr., 23, and Juan Infante, 47, and charged them with several crimes, including criminal possession of a controlled substance, after seizing 10 kilograms of heroin that was hidden in a compartment inside a wall.
Patrick J. Brackley, a lawyer who represented Mr. Mercedes and his son and Mr. Cruz Francisco at arraignment on Tuesday, said there “needs to be more investigation” into the government’s case.
“They’re seemingly charged in the same conspiracy, but when the evidence comes out, it will be a different story,” Mr. Brackley said. “They have cast a very wide net.”
All but the elder Mr. Mercedes are legal permanent residents of the United States, a law enforcement official said.
On Tuesday, on West 251st Street, residents said the area, though just north of the prestigious private school Horace Mann and Manhattan College, was a bit rougher than the neighborhood’s tonier corners.
Pauline LaCambra, 45, a nurse at St. Joseph’s Medical Center who lives near the site of the arrests, said a nearby gas station had been robbed repeatedly before being shut down. It is now covered in graffiti.
“The outskirts here,” she said of the area, “are different.”
Jonathan Chickavelli, 48, who lives in an apartment next to Apartment 5E, said that he had seen its occupants only twice since the end of March and that he never suspected that such an operation was being run so close to his home. Yet, he said, it made sense.
“It seems like that’s like a trend,” he said. “That’s like a thing they’re doing now. You know, you stay away from where the hot spots are and you go into a nice neighborhood and hide.”
Correction: May 19, 2015
Because of an editing error, an earlier version of a headline misstated where law enforcement officials found 155 pounds of heroin. As the article noted correctly, it was in a vehicle, not an apartment.
Correction: May 20, 2015
Because of an editing error, an earlier version of a capsule summary with this article referred incorrectly to the seizure of heroin in the Bronx. As the article correctly notes, it was the largest amount of heroin confiscated by the Drug Enforcement Administration in New York City, not the largest amount ever intercepted in the city.
